talks.title: Ghost on the Wire
talks.teaser: hoodiepony discusses digital privacy, operational security, and network footprint reduction in virtual reality and connected cyberspace.
talks.summary:
In this virtual presentation for DEF CON 31 DCGVR, security researcher Hoodie Pony presents "Ghost on the Wire," demonstrating how to construct out-of-band covert command-and-control (C2) channels over radio frequencies when traditional network egress is completely locked down. At 04:00, he configures an isolated virtual machine with all virtual network adapters severed, demonstrating that network-isolated environments remain vulnerable to RF-based signaling.

Hoodie Pony introduces Software-Defined Radios (SDRs) at 08:00, showing how attackers can transmit covert data payloads directly to target hosts. At 16:00, he leverages amateur radio infrastructure, broadcasting encoded AX.25 packets over the 2-meter band (144.390 MHz) using the Automatic Packet Reporting System (APRS). At 20:00, he details configuring the Dire Wolf software soundcard TNC to modulate and demodulate packet radio signals. He concludes at 24:00 by evaluating defensive countermeasures, emphasizing RF shielding and physical perimeter controls in high-security facilities. (AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Hey Crypto Bro
talks.teaser: Sam Colaizzi examines cryptocurrency hype, blockchain security pitfalls, and realistic threat models for decentralized systems.
talks.summary:
Sam Colaizzi delivers an exhaustive, critical analysis of cybersecurity threats across the cryptocurrency and decentralized finance (DeFi) ecosystem in "Hey Crypto Bro," presented at the DEF CON 31 DCGVR Village.

[15:52] Colaizzi evaluates the threat models of various cryptocurrency storage solutions, contrasting non-custodial hardware wallets (Coldcard, Ledger, Trezor) with software hot wallets and centralized exchanges. He dissects the dark web cybercriminal economy [30:18], analyzing specialized threat actor forums where stolen seed phrases, malware logs, and compromised exchange accounts are routinely traded.

[44:33] The presentation examines massive state-sponsored cyber operations targeting the blockchain sector, focusing on North Korean advanced persistent threat groups (such as Lazarus Group / APT38) responsible for stealing billions of dollars through sophisticated cross-chain bridge hacks and smart contract exploits (including the Ronin and Harmony bridge compromises). Colaizzi breaks down specific smart contract attack vectors [58:58]—such as reentrancy, flash loan price manipulation, and compromised multi-sig keys—concluding with defensive best practices for securing digital assets.

talks.title: Bootsquad
talks.teaser: Joe Mast highlights grassroots organizing and community mentorship initiatives across DEF CON Groups.
talks.summary:
In this operational security briefing for DEF CON 31 DCGVR, Joe M., a security engineer at CrowdStrike, delivers a comprehensive guide to brand protection, combatting typosquatting, and arbitrating fraudulent domain registrations. At 07:00, he outlines the dispute lifecycle, breaking down the seven procedural phases required to build an evidentiary case against trademark infringers.

Joe contrasts dispute mechanisms at 14:00, comparing the Uniform Domain-Name Dispute-Resolution Policy (UDRP) with the Uniform Rapid Suspension (URS) system, explaining that URS offers an expedited, cost-effective avenue ($300-$500) to freeze abusive domains rapidly without costly legal proceedings. At 28:00, he discusses techniques for piercing WHOIS privacy proxies during fraud investigations. He finishes at 35:00 by detailing enterprise domain registrar hardening, recommending registry locking and phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication to prevent unauthorized domain hijacks. talks.title: The Curse of the Ncurses
talks.teaser: JBO explores the quirks, historical bugs, and text user interface development challenges in ncurses.
talks.summary:
Security researcher JBO presents a deep technical vulnerability research case study in "The Curse of the Ncurses," detailing multiple memory corruption vulnerabilities discovered during a code audit of GNU ncurses and the terminfo terminal capabilities database.

[09:19] JBO explains the historical complexity and stack-based virtual machine architecture of ncurses terminfo string parsing. Terminfo files define terminal capabilities using a specialized bytecode language with an internal evaluation stack [18:07], allowing terminal drivers to push parameters, manipulate strings, and calculate dynamic offsets.

[26:51] The talk explores the attack surface of flawed format string and parameter expansion logic in ncurses capabilities (such as %p, %d, %s, and %v specifiers [35:59]). JBO demonstrates how crafted terminfo descriptions can trigger out-of-bounds stack reads, heap overflows, and memory corruption, highlighting how unprivileged local attackers can exploit vulnerable terminal libraries to target setuid binaries and terminal emulators.
